extracted.intended_audience: advertisers, marketers, public-relations professionals, students and researchers interested in advertising ethics and effectiveness
extracted.subtask_description: Identify, evaluate, or design advertising that deliberately startles or offends by violating social norms; consider content types, intended effects, audience perception, legal and branding consequences. Useful for analyzing campaigns (e.g., Benetton, Calvin Klein) or assessing whether shock tactics are appropriate and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate norm violation to startle or offend
rubrics_metrics.description: Shock advertising 'deliberately, rather than inadvertently, startles and offends its audience by violating norms for social values and personal ideals'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: intent to offend/startle through deliberate breach of social values or personal ideals. Use this to distinguish shock advertising from accidentally offensive ads. Example: campaigns that intentionally provoke outrage to get attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of graphic imagery and blunt slogans
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the employment in advertising or public relations of 'graphic imagery and blunt slogans to highlight' a public policy issue, goods, or services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: presence of highly explicit visual elements and direct, uncompromising copy. Examples include gore, diseased organs, or stark textual slogans. Anti-pattern: mild or ambiguous imagery that lacks blunt messaging—may fail to register as 'shock'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purpose: break through clutter and create buzz
rubrics_metrics.description: Shock advertising is designed principally to break through the advertising 'clutter' to capture attention and create buzz, and also to attract an audience to a certain brand or bring awareness to a certain public service issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the ad's core objective is attention-generation/awareness rather than subtle brand-building. Scoring: high if the ad clearly targets salience and conversation, lower if shock is incidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversial, disturbing, explicit, and crass content
rubrics_metrics.description: This form of advertising is often controversial, disturbing, explicit and crass, and may entail bold and provocative political messages that challenge the public’s conventional understanding of the social order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to judge tone and expected public reaction. Examples include politically provocative imagery, explicitly sexual or grotesque content. Note that controversy can be purposeful but also harmful to brand equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fear and scare tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: This form of advertising may not only offend but can also frighten as well, using scare tactics and elements of fear to sell a product or deliver a public service message, making a 'high impact.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether fear appeals are central to the message. Consider appropriateness for target audience (e.g., children may be vulnerable) and potential for regulatory backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of norm violations/content categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Shock advertisements can include disregard for tradition, law or practice (e.g., lewd or tasteless sexual references or obscenity), defiance of the social or moral code (e.g., vulgarity, brutality, nudity, feces, or profanity) or the display of images or words that are horrifying, terrifying, or repulsive (e.g., gruesome or revolting scenes, or violence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catalog the specific shock mechanisms used (sexuality, bodily fluids, violence, profanity, etc.). Use these categories to anticipate complaints, censorship risks, and cultural sensitivity issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-related shock (the 'unmentionables')
rubrics_metrics.description: Some advertisements may be considered shocking... because the products themselves are 'unmentionables' not to be openly presented or discussed in the public sphere (examples: cigarettes, feminine hygiene products, contraceptives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether shock arises from product category rather than execution. Products like sexual-health services, weight-loss, funeral services, or gambling may provoke offense even with neutral creative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provocative language and brand naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Shocking advertising content may also entail improper or indecent language, like French Connection's 'fcuk' campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess word-level provocations (puns, deliberate misspellings, borderline profanity). Consider trademark/legal constraints and public tolerance for lexical provocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional appeals used within shock advertising (humor, sex, fear)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shock advertising could also refer to the usage of emotional appeals such as humor, sex or fear. Humor has for a long time been the most frequently used communication tool within advertising, and according to branch active people it is considered to be the most effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine which emotional lever the ad relies on. Note that humor can coexist with shock and may increase effectiveness, but misjudged humor risks trivializing serious issues or escalating offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness metrics: attention, memory, and behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: One finding suggests 'shocking content in an advertisement significantly increases attention, benefits memory, and positively influences behavior.' The same study also shows that consumers are more likely to remember shocking advertising content over advertising content that is not shocking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating impact, measure attention (recall/recognition), memory retention, and behavioral influence (e.g., calls to action, attitude change). Balanced scoring should weigh short-term salience vs. longer-term consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience perceptual filters and perceptual defense
rubrics_metrics.description: The effects of shock advertising could also be explained by the theory of selective perception... Perceptual defense is the tendency for people to protect themselves against ideas, objects or situations that are threatening. This means that if a consumer finds a certain kind of advertising content threatening or disturbing, this message will be filtered out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the target audience is likely to engage or to defensively ignore the ad. Example: heavy smokers may filter out images of diseased lungs, reducing effectiveness. Include segmentation and prior-experience filters in assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential long-term branding consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A company could suffer long term branding issues if using shock advertising as a communication method. Using shocking pictures could affect the way consumers perceive a brand and quality of their product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess brand-fit and long-term equity risks: alienation of core customers, perceived decline in product quality, or reputational damage. Score high risk when shock contradicts established brand values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and regulatory constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal advertising that employs shockvertising would depict or re-enact a car accident, which is now illegal in New York. (Other jurisdictions may have bans or restrictions; campaigns have resulted in complaints and removals.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check jurisdiction-specific laws and ad-regulator codes (e.g., bans on reenacting accidents, limits on sexualized imagery of minors). Factor likely complaints, removals, or fines into any evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural and contextual variability in reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Shockvertising is recognized around the world... but reception and acceptability vary by culture and context (examples: Benetton campaigns praised for raising awareness and also denounced for historical connotations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate cross-cultural meanings and historical connotations. Examples: an image celebrated in one culture may be taboo in another; past historical associations (e.g., racial history) can change interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of high-impact documentary or realistic imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include use of blood and gore, diseased organs and human body parts... a newborn infant still attached to its umbilical cord, an image of a man dying of AIDS, a soldier holding a human bone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess realism and documentary-style presentations that amplify perceived authenticity and shock. Such realism may increase attention but also intensify complaints and ethical scrutiny—evaluate necessity and proportionality.
